title: Chapter 1
paragraphs: The Principle of the Commercial or Mercantile System

The idea that wealth consists of money, or of gold and silver, is a popular one, and it arises naturally from money's two functions: it is the instrument of commerce and the measure of value. Because money is the instrument of commerce, having it lets us get whatever else we need more easily than any other commodity could. The great task is always to get money. Once that is done, no later purchase is hard to make. Because money is also the measure of value, we judge the worth of every other commodity by the amount of money it will exchange for. We say that a rich man is worth a great deal of money and a poor man very little. A thrifty man, or one eager to be rich, is said to love money, while a careless, generous, or extravagant man is said to be indifferent to it. To grow rich is to get money, and in everyday speech wealth and money are treated as completely interchangeable.

A rich country, like a rich man, is assumed to be one full of money, and piling up gold and silver is assumed to be the quickest way to enrich it. For a while after America was discovered, whenever the Spaniards landed on an unknown coast their first question was whether any gold or silver could be found nearby. From the answers they got, they judged whether the place was worth settling or the country worth conquering. Plano Carpino, a monk sent as ambassador by the king of France to one of the sons of the famous Genghis Khan, reports that the Tartars often asked him whether the kingdom of France had plenty of sheep and oxen. Their question had the same purpose as the Spaniards'. They wanted to know whether the country was rich enough to be worth conquering. Among the Tartars, as among all other nations of herdsmen, who generally know nothing of money, cattle serve as the instruments of commerce and the measures of value. So for them wealth consisted in cattle, just as for the Spaniards it consisted in gold and silver. Of the two views, the Tartar one was perhaps closer to the truth.

Locke points out a difference between money and other movable goods. All other movable goods, he says, are so easily consumed that the wealth they make up cannot be relied on; a nation rich in them one year may, without exporting any, simply through its own waste and extravagance, badly need them the next. Money, by contrast, is a steady friend: it may pass from hand to hand, but as long as it can be kept from leaving the country it is not easily wasted or used up. Gold and silver, on his view, are therefore the most solid and lasting part of a nation's movable wealth, and so he thinks the great aim of its economic policy should be to multiply those metals.

Others concede that if a nation could be cut off from the rest of the world, the amount of money circulating in it would make no difference. The consumable goods that money helps to circulate would simply exchange for more or fewer coins, but the country's real wealth or poverty would depend entirely on whether those consumable goods were plentiful or scarce. The case is different, they think, for countries that have dealings with foreign nations and that must fight foreign wars and keep fleets and armies in distant places. This, they say, cannot be done except by sending money abroad to pay for it, and a nation cannot send much money abroad unless it has plenty at home. Every such nation, then, must try in peacetime to build up gold and silver, so that when the need arises it has the means to wage war abroad.

Acting on these popular notions, all the different nations of Europe have tried, with little success, every possible way of accumulating gold and silver within their borders. Spain and Portugal, which own the chief mines that supply Europe with these metals, have either banned their export under the harshest penalties or charged a heavy duty on it. A similar ban seems in earlier times to have been part of most other European nations' policy. It even turns up where we would least expect it, in some old Scottish acts of Parliament that forbid carrying gold or silver out of the kingdom under heavy penalties. The same policy once applied in both France and England.

When these countries became commercial, their merchants often found the ban extremely inconvenient. They could frequently buy the foreign goods they wanted, whether to import into their own country or to carry on to another foreign one, more cheaply with gold and silver than with any other commodity. So they protested against the ban as harmful to trade.

First, they argued that exporting gold and silver to buy foreign goods did not always reduce the quantity of those metals in the kingdom; on the contrary, it might often increase it. If the country's consumption of foreign goods was not raised as a result, those goods could be re-exported to other countries and sold there for a large profit, bringing back far more treasure than had originally been sent out to buy them. Mun compares this working of foreign trade to the sowing and harvest of farming. “If we only look,” he says, “at what the farmer does at sowing time, when he throws away much good corn into the ground, we will think him a madman rather than a farmer. But when we consider his work at harvest, the goal of all his effort, we find the value and the abundant increase in what he has done.”

Second, they argued that the ban could not actually stop the export of gold and silver, which, being so small in bulk relative to their value, could easily be smuggled out. The only way to prevent such export, they said, was to pay proper attention to what they called the balance of trade. When a country exported more in value than it imported, a balance was owed to it by foreign nations, which had to be paid in gold and silver, and this increased the quantity of those metals in the kingdom. But when it imported more in value than it exported, the opposite balance was owed to foreign nations, which had to be paid the same way, and this reduced that quantity. In that case, banning the export of these metals could not stop it but would only make it more dangerous and therefore more expensive. The exchange rate was thereby turned more against the country that owed the balance than it otherwise would have been, because the merchant who bought a bill on the foreign country had to pay the banker who sold it not only for the natural risk, trouble, and cost of sending the money there, but also for the extra risk created by the ban. And the more the exchange ran against any country, the more the balance of trade necessarily ran against it too, since that country's money became worth so much less compared with the money of the country to which the balance was owed. If the exchange between England and Holland, for example, stood at five per cent against England, it would take 105 ounces of silver in England to buy a bill for 100 ounces of silver in Holland. So 105 ounces of silver in England would be worth only 100 ounces in Holland and would buy only a proportional quantity of Dutch goods, while 100 ounces of silver in Holland would be worth 105 ounces in England and would buy a proportional quantity of English goods. The English goods sold to Holland would go that much cheaper, and the Dutch goods sold to England that much dearer, by the amount of the exchange difference. The one would draw that much less Dutch money to England, and the other that much more English money to Holland, by the same amount. So the balance of trade would necessarily run that much further against England and would require a greater balance of gold and silver to be exported to Holland.

These arguments were partly sound and partly false. They were sound in claiming that exporting gold and silver in trade could often benefit the country. They were sound, too, in claiming that no ban could prevent the export of these metals when private individuals found it profitable to send them out. But they were false in supposing that preserving or increasing the quantity of these metals required more attention from the government than preserving or increasing the quantity of any other useful commodity, which free trade, with no such attention, never fails to supply in the right amount. They were perhaps false, too, in claiming that a high exchange rate necessarily worsened what they called the unfavourable balance of trade, or caused a greater quantity of gold and silver to be exported. That high rate was indeed very disadvantageous to merchants who had money to pay abroad, since they paid that much more for the bills their bankers granted them on those countries. But although the risk created by the ban might cost the bankers something extra, it would not necessarily carry any more money out of the country. That extra expense would generally all be spent within the country, on smuggling the money out, and could rarely cause the export of a single sixpence beyond the exact sum drawn for. A high exchange rate would also naturally lead merchants to try to make their exports roughly balance their imports, so that they had to pay this costly exchange on as small a sum as possible. Besides, a high exchange rate must necessarily have acted as a tax, raising the price of foreign goods and so reducing their consumption. It would therefore tend not to increase but to decrease what they called the unfavourable balance of trade, and consequently the export of gold and silver.

Such as they were, however, these arguments convinced the people they were aimed at. They were put by merchants to parliaments and to the councils of princes, to nobles, and to country gentlemen: by people thought to understand trade, to people who knew they themselves understood nothing of it. That foreign trade enriched the country was something experience proved to the nobles and country gentlemen as well as to the merchants, but how, or in what way, none of them really knew. The merchants knew perfectly well how it enriched themselves, since that was their business to know. But how it enriched the country was no part of their business. The question never crossed their minds except when they had occasion to ask the country for some change in the laws governing foreign trade. Then it became necessary to say something about the benefits of foreign trade and how those benefits were blocked by the laws as they stood. To the judges who were to decide the matter, it seemed a thoroughly satisfactory account when they were told that foreign trade brought money into the country but that the laws in question kept it from bringing in as much as it otherwise would. So these arguments produced the desired effect. In France and England, the ban on exporting gold and silver was confined to the coin of those countries. Exporting foreign coin and bullion was made free. In Holland and some other places, this freedom was extended even to the country's own coin. The government's attention was turned away from preventing the export of gold and silver and toward watching the balance of trade, as the only thing that could cause those metals to increase or decrease. From one useless concern it was turned to another that was far more complicated, far more troublesome, and just as useless. The title of Mun's book, England's Treasure by Foreign Trade, became a basic maxim of economic policy not only in England but in every other commercial country. The inland or home trade, the most important of all, the trade in which an equal amount of capital yields the greatest revenue and creates the most employment for the country's people, was treated as merely secondary to foreign trade. It brought no money into the country, people said, nor carried any out. So the country, they thought, could never grow either richer or poorer through it, except insofar as its rise or decline might indirectly affect the state of foreign trade.

A country with no mines of its own must of course draw its gold and silver from abroad, just as a country with no vineyards must draw its wines. There seems no reason, though, why the government should pay more attention to the one than to the other. A country with the means to buy wine will always get the wine it needs, and a country with the means to buy gold and silver will never be short of those metals. They are bought for a certain price, like all other commodities, and just as they are the price of all other commodities, so all other commodities are the price of them. We trust, with complete confidence, that free trade, without any government attention, will always supply us with the wine we need; and we may trust with equal confidence that it will always supply us with all the gold and silver we can afford to buy or to use, whether in circulating our goods or for other purposes.

The quantity of any commodity that human industry can either buy or produce regulates itself naturally in every country according to the effective demand, that is, the demand of those willing to pay the whole of the rent, labour, and profit that must be paid to prepare it and bring it to market. But no commodities regulate themselves more easily or more exactly by this effective demand than gold and silver, because, being small in bulk and great in value, no commodities can be moved more easily from place to place: from where they are cheap to where they are dear, from where they are in surplus to where they fall short of this effective demand. If there were in England, for example, an effective demand for an additional quantity of gold, a packet-boat could bring from Lisbon, or from wherever else it could be had, fifty tons of gold, which could be coined into more than five million guineas. But if there were an effective demand for grain of the same value, importing it would require, at five guineas a ton, a million tons of shipping, or a thousand ships of a thousand tons each. The whole navy of England would not be enough.

When the quantity of gold and silver imported into a country exceeds the effective demand, no government vigilance can stop their export. All the savage laws of Spain and Portugal cannot keep their gold and silver at home. The constant imports from Peru and Brazil exceed the effective demand of those countries and push the price of these metals there below their price in neighbouring countries. If, on the other hand, in some particular country their quantity fell short of the effective demand, raising their price above that in neighbouring countries, the government would have no need to take any trouble to import them. Even if it did take trouble to prevent their import, it could not succeed. Once the Spartans had the means to buy these metals, they broke through every barrier that the laws of Lycurgus set against their entry into Lacedaemon. All the savage customs laws cannot prevent the import of tea from the Dutch and Gothenburg East India companies, because it is somewhat cheaper than the British company's tea. A pound of tea, however, is about a hundred times the bulk of one of the highest prices, sixteen shillings, that is commonly paid for it in silver, and more than two thousand times the bulk of the same price in gold, and so just that many times harder to smuggle.

It is partly because gold and silver are so easily moved from places where they are plentiful to places where they are wanted that their price does not fluctuate constantly, as the price of most other commodities does, since those are too bulky to shift location when the market happens to be over- or under-stocked with them. The price of these metals is not entirely free from change, but the changes it undergoes are generally slow, gradual, and steady. In Europe, for example, it is supposed, perhaps without much basis, that during this century and the last they have been constantly but gradually falling in value because of the continual imports from the Spanish West Indies. But to make any sudden change in the price of gold and silver, raising or lowering all at once, sharply and noticeably, the money price of every other commodity, requires an upheaval in commerce like the one caused by the discovery of America.

If, in spite of all this, gold and silver should at some time fall short in a country that has the means to buy them, there are more ways to replace them than there are for almost any other commodity. If the raw materials of manufacture are lacking, industry must stop. If food is lacking, the people must starve. But if money is lacking, barter will take its place, though with a good deal of inconvenience. Buying and selling on credit, with the various dealers settling their accounts against one another once a month or once a year, will replace it with less inconvenience. A well-regulated paper money will replace it not only without any inconvenience but, in some cases, with real advantages. On every count, then, the government's attention was never so needlessly employed as when directed to watching over the preservation or increase of the quantity of money in a country.

Yet no complaint is more common than that money is scarce. Money, like wine, must always be scarce for those who have neither the means to buy it nor the credit to borrow it. Those who have either will seldom lack the money, or the wine, they need. This complaint of a scarcity of money is not always confined to reckless spendthrifts. It is sometimes general throughout a whole commercial town and the surrounding countryside. Over-trading is the usual cause of it. Sober men, whose ventures have outrun their capital, are just as likely to have neither the means to buy money nor the credit to borrow it as spendthrifts whose spending has outrun their income. Before their ventures can pay off, their stock is gone, and their credit with it. They run about everywhere trying to borrow money, and everyone tells them there is none to lend. Even such general complaints of a scarcity of money do not always prove that the usual number of gold and silver coins are not circulating in the country; they prove rather that many people want those coins who have nothing to give for them. When the profits of trade happen to be greater than usual, over-trading becomes a general error among dealers great and small. They do not always send more money abroad than usual, but they buy on credit, both at home and abroad, an unusual quantity of goods, which they send to some distant market in the hope that the returns will come in before payment is due. The bill comes due before the returns arrive, and they have nothing on hand with which to buy money or to give solid security for a loan. It is not any scarcity of gold and silver, but the difficulty such people have in borrowing, and the difficulty their creditors have in getting paid, that causes the general complaint of a scarcity of money.

It would be too absurd to set about seriously proving that wealth does not consist in money, or in gold and silver, but in what money buys, and is valuable only for buying. Money, no doubt, always makes up part of the national capital; but it has already been shown that it generally makes up only a small part, and always the least profitable part, of it.

It is not because wealth consists more essentially in money than in goods that the merchant generally finds it easier to buy goods with money than to buy money with goods. It is because money is the known and established instrument of commerce, for which everything is readily given in exchange, but which is not always so readily got in exchange for everything. Besides, most goods are more perishable than money, and the merchant may often suffer a much greater loss by holding them. When his goods are on hand, too, he is more exposed to demands for money that he may be unable to meet than when he has their price in his coffers. On top of all this, his profit comes more directly from selling than from buying; so for all these reasons he is generally far more anxious to exchange his goods for money than his money for goods. But although a particular merchant, with plenty of goods in his warehouse, may sometimes be ruined by failing to sell them in time, a nation or country is not exposed to the same accident. A merchant's whole capital often consists of perishable goods meant for buying money. But only a very small part of a country's annual produce of land and labour can ever be meant for buying gold and silver from its neighbours. By far the greater part is circulated and consumed among themselves, and even of the surplus that is sent abroad, the greater part is generally meant for buying other foreign goods. So even if gold and silver could not be got in exchange for the goods meant to buy them, the nation would not be ruined. It might indeed suffer some loss and inconvenience and be forced into some of the expedients needed to replace money. But the annual produce of its land and labour would stay the same, or very nearly the same, as usual, because the same, or very nearly the same, consumable capital would be employed in maintaining it. And although goods do not always draw money as readily as money draws goods, in the long run they draw it more surely than money draws them. Goods can serve many purposes besides buying money, but money can serve no purpose besides buying goods. So money necessarily runs after goods, but goods do not always or necessarily run after money. The man who buys does not always mean to sell again, but often to use or consume; whereas the man who sells always means to buy again. The one may often have done the whole of his business, but the other can never have done more than half of his. It is not for its own sake that men want money, but for the sake of what they can buy with it.

Consumable goods, it is said, are soon destroyed, whereas gold and silver are more durable, and but for this constant export could be accumulated for ages on end, hugely increasing the country's real wealth. So, the claim goes, nothing can be more disadvantageous to a country than a trade that exchanges such lasting goods for such perishable ones. Yet we do not count it disadvantageous to exchange English hardware for French wines, even though hardware is a very durable commodity and, but for this constant export, could likewise be accumulated for ages on end, hugely increasing the country's stock of pots and pans. But it readily occurs to us that the number of such utensils in any country is necessarily limited by the use there is for them; that it would be absurd to have more pots and pans than are needed for cooking the food usually consumed there; and that, if the quantity of food were to increase, the number of pots and pans would readily increase with it, part of the extra food being used to buy them or to maintain extra workers whose job it is to make them. It should occur to us just as readily that the quantity of gold and silver in any country is limited by the use there is for those metals; that their use lies in circulating goods, as coin, and in providing a kind of household furniture, as plate; that the quantity of coin in any country is regulated by the value of the goods it is to circulate, so that if you increase that value, part of the coin will at once be sent abroad to buy, wherever it can be had, the extra coin needed to circulate them; and that the quantity of plate is regulated by the number and wealth of the private families who choose to indulge in that kind of magnificence, so that if you increase the number and wealth of such families, part of this added wealth will most likely be spent buying, wherever it can be found, an additional quantity of plate. To try to increase a country's wealth either by bringing in or by keeping in it an unnecessary quantity of gold and silver is as absurd as trying to improve the dinners of private families by forcing them to keep an unnecessary number of kitchen utensils. Just as the cost of buying those unnecessary utensils would reduce, not increase, either the quantity or the quality of the family's food, so the cost of buying an unnecessary quantity of gold and silver must, in every country, just as surely reduce the wealth that feeds, clothes, and houses, that maintains and employs, the people. Gold and silver, whether as coin or as plate, are utensils, it must be remembered, just as much as the furniture of the kitchen. Increase the use of them, increase the consumable goods that are to be circulated, managed, and prepared by means of them, and you will infallibly increase their quantity; but if you try by extraordinary means to increase their quantity, you will just as infallibly reduce their use, and even their quantity too, since the quantity of these metals can never be greater than what their use requires. Were they ever accumulated beyond this quantity, their transport is so easy, and the loss from their lying idle and unused so great, that no law could stop them from being sent straight out of the country.

It is not always necessary to accumulate gold and silver to enable a country to wage foreign wars and keep fleets and armies in distant places. Fleets and armies are maintained not with gold and silver but with consumable goods. The nation that, out of the annual produce of its home industry, out of the annual revenue from its lands, labour, and consumable stock, has the means to buy those consumable goods in distant countries can wage foreign wars there.

A nation can buy the pay and provisions of an army in a distant country in three different ways: by sending abroad, first, some part of its accumulated gold and silver; or, second, some part of the annual produce of its manufactures; or, last, some part of its annual raw produce.

The gold and silver that can properly be regarded as accumulated, or stored up, in a country may be divided into three parts: first, the circulating money; second, the plate of private families; and last, the money that may have been gathered through many years of saving and laid up in the prince's treasury.

Little can usually be spared from the country's circulating money, because there is seldom much surplus in it. The value of goods bought and sold each year in any country requires a certain quantity of money to circulate and distribute them to their proper consumers, and can employ no more. The channel of circulation necessarily draws to itself just enough to fill it, and never takes any more. In the case of a foreign war, however, something is usually withdrawn from this channel. Since many people are maintained abroad, fewer are maintained at home. Fewer goods circulate there, and less money is needed to circulate them. An extra quantity of paper money of some sort, too, such as exchequer notes, navy bills, and bank bills in England, is generally issued on such occasions, and by taking the place of circulating gold and silver it makes it possible to send more of those metals abroad. All this, however, could provide only a poor resource for waging a foreign war of great expense and several years' duration.

Melting down the plate of private families has, on every occasion, proved an even more trivial resource. The French, at the start of the last war, did not gain enough from this expedient to make up for the loss of the workmanship.

The accumulated treasure of the prince has in earlier times provided a much greater and more lasting resource. In our own day, with the exception of the king of Prussia, accumulating treasure seems to be no part of the policy of European princes.

The funds that paid for this century's foreign wars, perhaps the most expensive that history records, seem to have depended little on exporting either the circulating money, or the plate of private families, or the treasure of the prince. The last French war cost Great Britain more than £90,000,000, including not only the £75,000,000 of new debt that was contracted, but the additional two shillings in the pound of land tax, and what was borrowed each year from the sinking fund. More than two-thirds of this expense was spent in distant countries: in Germany, Portugal, and America, in the ports of the Mediterranean, and in the East and West Indies. The kings of England had no accumulated treasure. We never heard of any extraordinary quantity of plate being melted down. The circulating gold and silver of the country had not been thought to exceed £18,000,000. Since the recent recoinage of the gold, however, that figure is believed to have been considerably underestimated. Let us suppose, then, on the most exaggerated estimate I can recall ever seeing or hearing, that gold and silver together came to £30,000,000. Had the war been waged by means of our money, all of it must, even on this estimate, have been sent out and brought back again at least twice in a period of six or seven years. If we suppose this, it gives the most decisive argument to show how needless it is for government to watch over the preservation of money, since on this supposition the whole money of the country must have left it and returned to it twice in so short a period without anyone knowing anything about it. Yet the channel of circulation never appeared emptier than usual during any part of this period. Few people who had the means to pay for money lacked it. The profits of foreign trade were indeed greater than usual throughout the war, and especially toward its end. This caused, as it always does, a general over-trading in all the ports of Great Britain, and this in turn caused the usual complaint of a scarcity of money, which always follows over-trading. Many people wanted money who had neither the means to buy it nor the credit to borrow it; and because debtors found it hard to borrow, creditors found it hard to get paid. Gold and silver, however, were generally to be had for their value by anyone who had that value to give for them.

The enormous expense of the late war, then, must have been met chiefly not by exporting gold and silver but by exporting British goods of one kind or another. When the government, or those acting under it, contracted with a merchant for a remittance to some foreign country, he would naturally try to pay the foreign correspondent on whom he drew a bill by sending goods abroad rather than gold and silver. If British goods were not in demand in that country, he would try to send them to some other country where he could buy a bill on the first one. Transporting goods, when they are well suited to the market, always brings a considerable profit, whereas transporting gold and silver almost never does. When these metals are sent abroad to buy foreign goods, the merchant's profit comes not from the purchase but from the sale of the returns. But when they are sent abroad merely to pay a debt, he gets no returns and so no profit. So he naturally exercises his ingenuity to find a way of paying his foreign debts by exporting goods rather than gold and silver. The great quantity of British goods exported during the late war without bringing back any returns is accordingly noted by the author of The Present State of the Nation.

Besides the three sorts of gold and silver mentioned above, there is in every great commercial country a good deal of bullion imported and exported in turn for the purposes of foreign trade. As this bullion circulates among different commercial countries, in the same way that a nation's coin circulates within it, it may be regarded as the money of the great commercial republic. National coin gets its movement and direction from the goods circulated within the bounds of each particular country; the money of the commercial republic, from the goods circulated between different countries. Both are employed in making exchanges easier: the one between different individuals of the same nation, the other between individuals of different nations. Part of this money of the great commercial republic may have been, and probably was, used in waging the late war. In a general war, it is natural to suppose that this money is given a movement and direction different from what it usually follows in deep peace, so that it circulates more around the seat of the war and is used more to buy, there and in the neighbouring countries, the pay and provisions of the various armies. But whatever part of this money of the commercial republic Great Britain may have employed each year in this way, it must have been bought each year either with British goods, or with something else that had been bought with them, which brings us back again to goods, to the annual produce of the country's land and labour, as the ultimate resource that enabled us to wage the war. It is natural, indeed, to suppose that so great an annual expense must have been met out of a great annual produce. The expense of 1761, for example, came to more than £19,000,000. No accumulated store could have sustained so great an annual outpouring. There is no annual produce, even of gold and silver, that could have sustained it. The whole gold and silver imported each year into both Spain and Portugal, by the best accounts, does not usually much exceed £6,000,000 sterling, which in some years would scarcely have paid four months' expense of the late war.

The goods best suited for transport to distant countries, in order to buy there either the pay and provisions of an army, or some part of the money of the commercial republic to be used in buying them, seem to be the finer and more refined manufactures, the kind that pack great value into small bulk and can therefore be exported a great distance at little cost. A country whose industry produces a great annual surplus of such manufactures, usually exported to foreign countries, can wage a very expensive foreign war for many years without exporting any considerable quantity of gold and silver, or even having any such quantity to export. In this case a considerable part of its annual surplus of manufactures must indeed be exported without bringing back any returns to the country, though it does bring returns to the merchant, since the government buys from the merchant his bills on foreign countries in order to buy there the pay and provisions of an army. Some part of this surplus, however, may still bring back a return. During the war the manufacturers will face a double demand and be called on, first, to work up goods to be sent abroad to pay the bills drawn on foreign countries for the army's pay and provisions, and, second, to work up the goods needed to buy the ordinary returns usually consumed in the country. So in the midst of the most destructive foreign war, the greater part of manufactures may often flourish greatly, and, on the contrary, may decline when peace returns. They may flourish amid their country's ruin and begin to decay when its prosperity returns. The varying state of many different branches of British manufacture during the late war, and for some time after the peace, may serve to illustrate what has just been said.

No foreign war of great expense or duration could conveniently be waged by exporting the raw produce of the soil. The cost of sending abroad enough of it to buy the pay and provisions of an army would be too great. Few countries, too, produce much more raw produce than is enough to feed their own inhabitants. To send any great quantity of it abroad, then, would be to send abroad part of the people's necessary food. It is otherwise with the export of manufactures. The upkeep of the people employed in them stays at home, and only the surplus part of their work is exported. Hume often notes the inability of the ancient kings of England to wage, without interruption, any long foreign war. The English in those days had nothing with which to buy the pay and provisions of their armies abroad except either the raw produce of the soil, of which no considerable part could be spared from home consumption, or a few of the coarsest manufactures, the transport of which, like that of the raw produce, was too expensive. This inability arose not from a lack of money but from a lack of the finer and more refined manufactures. Buying and selling were carried on by means of money in England then as well as now. The quantity of circulating money must have borne the same proportion to the number and value of purchases and sales usually transacted at that time as it does to those transacted now, or rather a greater proportion, because there was then no paper, which now takes over much of the work of gold and silver. Among nations that know little of commerce and manufactures, the sovereign, on extraordinary occasions, can seldom draw any considerable aid from his subjects, for reasons that will be explained later. So it is in such countries that he generally tries to accumulate a treasure, as the only resource against such emergencies. Quite apart from this necessity, in such a situation he is naturally inclined to the thrift that accumulation requires. In that simple state, even a sovereign's spending is not guided by the vanity that delights in the gaudy finery of a court, but is spent on generosity to his tenants and hospitality to his retainers. But generosity and hospitality very seldom lead to extravagance, though vanity almost always does. Every Tartar chief, accordingly, has a treasure. The treasures of Mazepa, chief of the Cossacks in Ukraine and the famous ally of Charles XII, are said to have been very great. The French kings of the Merovingian line all had treasures. When they divided their kingdom among their various children, they divided their treasures too. The Saxon princes, and the first kings after the Conquest, seem likewise to have accumulated treasures. The first act of every new reign was commonly to seize the treasure of the preceding king, as the most essential measure for securing the succession. The sovereigns of advanced commercial countries are not under the same necessity of accumulating treasures, because they can generally draw extraordinary aid from their subjects on extraordinary occasions. They are also less inclined to do so. They naturally, perhaps necessarily, follow the fashion of the times, and their spending comes to be governed by the same extravagant vanity that governs that of all the other great proprietors in their dominions. The trifling pageantry of their court grows more brilliant every day, and the cost of it not only prevents accumulation but often eats into the funds meant for more necessary expenses. What Dercyllidas said of the court of Persia may be applied to that of several European princes: that he saw there much splendour but little strength, many servants but few soldiers.

Importing gold and silver is not the chief, much less the only, benefit a nation gets from its foreign trade. Wherever foreign trade is carried on, all the places involved derive two distinct benefits from it. It carries out that surplus part of their land and labour's produce for which there is no demand among them, and brings back in return something else for which there is a demand. It gives a value to their surplus by exchanging it for something else that can satisfy part of their wants and increase their enjoyments. By means of it, the narrowness of the home market does not prevent the division of labour in any particular branch of art or manufacture from being carried to the highest perfection. By opening a wider market for whatever part of their labour's produce exceeds home consumption, it encourages them to improve its productive power and to raise its annual produce to the utmost, and so to increase the society's real revenue and wealth. These great and important services foreign trade is constantly performing for all the different countries between which it is carried on. They all gain greatly from it, though the country where the merchant lives generally gains the most, since he is generally more employed in supplying the wants and carrying out the surplus of his own country than of any other. To import the gold and silver that may be wanted into countries with no mines is, no doubt, part of the business of foreign commerce. It is, however, a most insignificant part of it. A country that carried on foreign trade merely on this account would scarcely have occasion to load a ship in a century.

It is not by importing gold and silver that the discovery of America has enriched Europe. Through the abundance of the American mines, those metals have become cheaper. A set of plate can now be bought for about a third of the corn, or a third of the labour, that it would have cost in the fifteenth century. With the same annual expense of labour and goods, Europe can now buy about three times the quantity of plate it could have bought then. But when a commodity comes to be sold for a third of what had been its usual price, not only can those who bought it before buy three times their former quantity, but it is brought within reach of a much greater number of buyers, perhaps more than ten, perhaps more than twenty, times the former number. So there may now be in Europe not only more than three times, but more than twenty or thirty times, the quantity of plate that would have been in it, even in its present state of improvement, had the American mines never been discovered. So far Europe has, no doubt, gained a real convenience, though surely a very trifling one. The cheapness of gold and silver makes these metals rather less fit for use as money than they were before. To make the same purchases, we must load ourselves with a greater quantity of them, and carry about a shilling in our pocket where a groat would have done before. It is hard to say which is the more trifling, this inconvenience or the opposite convenience. Neither could have made any very essential change in the state of Europe. The discovery of America, however, certainly did make a most essential one. By opening a new and inexhaustible market to all the goods of Europe, it gave rise to new divisions of labour and improvements of skill that could never have taken place within the narrow circle of the old commerce, for want of a market to absorb the greater part of their produce. The productive powers of labour were improved, and its produce increased, in all the different countries of Europe, and with it the real revenue and wealth of the inhabitants. The goods of Europe were almost all new to America, and many of those of America were new to Europe. So a new set of exchanges began that had never been thought of before, and that should naturally have proved as advantageous to the new continent as it certainly did to the old. The savage injustice of the Europeans turned an event that ought to have benefited all into one that was ruinous and destructive to several of those unfortunate countries.

The discovery of a passage to the East Indies by the Cape of Good Hope, which happened at about the same time, opened perhaps an even wider field to foreign commerce than even America did, despite the greater distance. There were only two nations in America in any respect superior to savages, and these were destroyed almost as soon as they were discovered. The rest were mere savages. But the empires of China, Hindustan, and Japan, as well as several others in the East Indies, though they had no richer mines of gold or silver, were in every other respect far richer, better cultivated, and more advanced in all arts and manufactures than either Mexico or Peru, even if we credit, what plainly deserves no credit, the exaggerated accounts of the Spanish writers about the ancient state of those empires. But rich and civilized nations can always exchange goods of much greater value with one another than with savages and barbarians. Europe, however, has so far gained much less from its trade with the East Indies than from that with America. The Portuguese monopolised the East India trade to themselves for about a century, and it was only indirectly, through them, that the other nations of Europe could send out or receive any goods from that country. When the Dutch, at the start of the last century, began to encroach on them, they placed their whole East India commerce in an exclusive company. The English, French, Swedes, and Danes have all followed their example, so that no great nation of Europe has yet had the benefit of free commerce to the East Indies. No other reason need be given why it has never been as advantageous as the trade to America, which, between almost every nation of Europe and its own colonies, is open to all its subjects. The exclusive privileges of those East India companies, their great riches, and the great favour and protection these have won them from their respective governments, have stirred much envy against them. This envy has often represented their trade as wholly pernicious, on account of the great quantities of silver it exports each year from the countries where it is carried on. The parties concerned have replied that their trade, by this constant export of silver, might indeed tend to impoverish Europe in general, but not the particular country from which the silver was carried, because, by re-exporting part of the returns to other European countries, it brought home each year a much greater quantity of that metal than it carried out. Both the objection and the reply rest on the popular notion I have just been examining. So there is no need to say anything more about either. Through the annual export of silver to the East Indies, plate is probably somewhat dearer in Europe than it might otherwise have been, and coined silver probably buys a larger quantity of both labour and goods. The first of these two effects is a very small loss, the second a very small advantage, both too insignificant to deserve any part of the public's attention. The trade to the East Indies, by opening a market to the goods of Europe, or, what comes to nearly the same thing, to the gold and silver bought with those goods, must necessarily tend to increase the annual production of European goods, and so the real wealth and revenue of Europe. That it has so far increased them so little is probably owing to the restraints it labours under everywhere.

I thought it necessary, at the risk of being tedious, to examine at full length this popular notion that wealth consists in money, or in gold and silver. In everyday speech, as I have already noted, money frequently means wealth, and this ambiguity of expression has made the popular notion so familiar to us that even those convinced of its absurdity are very apt to forget their own principles and, in the course of their reasoning, to take it for granted as a certain and undeniable truth. Some of the best English writers on commerce begin by observing that a country's wealth consists not in its gold and silver alone, but in its lands, houses, and consumable goods of every kind. In the course of their reasoning, however, the lands, houses, and consumable goods seem to slip from their memory, and the drift of their argument often supposes that all wealth consists in gold and silver, and that to multiply those metals is the great aim of national industry and commerce.

Once these two principles were established, however, that wealth consists in gold and silver, and that a country with no mines can bring in those metals only through the balance of trade, that is, by exporting more in value than it imports, it necessarily became the great aim of economic policy to reduce as much as possible the import of foreign goods for home consumption, and to increase as much as possible the export of home-produced goods. Its two great engines for enriching the country, therefore, were restraints on imports and encouragements to exports.
The restraints on imports were of two kinds.
First, restraints on importing such foreign goods for home consumption as could be produced at home, from whatever country they were imported.
Second, restraints on importing goods of almost every kind from those particular countries with which the balance of trade was supposed to be unfavourable.
These various restraints consisted sometimes in high duties and sometimes in outright bans.
Exports were encouraged sometimes by drawbacks, sometimes by bounties, sometimes by favourable trade treaties with foreign states, and sometimes by founding colonies in distant countries.

Drawbacks were given on two different occasions. When home manufactures were subject to any duty or excise, either the whole or part of it was frequently refunded on their export; and when foreign goods liable to a duty were imported in order to be exported again, either the whole or part of this duty was sometimes refunded on such export.
Bounties were given to encourage either some new manufactures or such other kinds of industry as were thought to deserve particular favour.
By favourable trade treaties, particular privileges were secured in some foreign state for the goods and merchants of the home country, beyond what was granted to those of other countries.
By founding colonies in distant countries, not only particular privileges but often a monopoly was secured for the goods and merchants of the country that founded them.

The two sorts of restraints on imports just mentioned, together with these four encouragements to exports, make up the six chief means by which the commercial system proposes to increase the quantity of gold and silver in a country by turning the balance of trade in its favour. I shall consider each of them in a separate chapter, and, without taking much further notice of their supposed tendency to bring money into the country, I shall examine chiefly what the likely effects of each are on the annual produce of its industry. According as they tend to increase or decrease the value of this annual produce, they must clearly tend to increase or decrease the real wealth and revenue of the country.

title: Chapter 2
paragraphs: Restraints on Importing Foreign Goods That Can Be Produced at Home.

When a country uses high duties or outright bans to keep out foreign goods that it could produce itself, it hands the domestic industry that makes those goods a near-monopoly over the home market. The ban on importing live cattle or salted meat, for instance, gives British graziers a monopoly on the home market for butcher's meat. The high duties on imported corn, which in years of moderate plenty amount to a ban, give corn growers the same kind of advantage. The ban on importing foreign woollens does the same for woollen manufacturers. The silk trade, even though it works entirely with foreign raw materials, has recently won the same protection. The linen trade has not yet won it but is moving quickly in that direction. Many other kinds of manufacturing in Britain have secured, either fully or nearly, a monopoly against their fellow citizens. Anyone who is not well versed in the customs laws would be astonished at the sheer range of goods whose importation into Britain is banned, either absolutely or under certain conditions.

There is no doubt that this monopoly of the home market often gives a strong boost to the particular industry that enjoys it, and that it often draws a larger share of both the society's labour and its capital toward that line of work than would otherwise have gone there. But whether it actually increases the total industry of the society, or steers it in the most advantageous direction, is perhaps not so obvious.

The total industry of a society can never be greater than what the society's capital can employ. Just as the number of workers any one person can keep employed must bear a fixed proportion to his capital, so the number that all the members of a great society can keep continuously employed must bear a fixed proportion to the society's whole capital, and it can never exceed that proportion. No regulation of trade can push the quantity of industry in any society beyond what its capital can sustain. All such a regulation can do is divert part of that industry into a channel it might not otherwise have entered, and there is no guarantee that this artificial direction is more advantageous to the society than the one industry would have chosen on its own.

Every individual works constantly to find the most profitable use for whatever capital he controls. What he has in view, of course, is his own advantage, not society's. Yet the pursuit of his own advantage naturally, or rather inevitably, leads him to prefer the use that happens to be most advantageous to society as well.

First, every individual tries to employ his capital as close to home as he can, and therefore as much as possible in supporting domestic industry, provided he can still earn the ordinary profit on his capital, or not much less than that.

So, where profits are equal or nearly equal, every wholesale merchant naturally prefers home trade to the foreign trade in consumer goods, and the foreign trade in consumer goods to the carrying trade. In the home trade his capital is never out of his sight for as long as it often is in the foreign trade. He can know better the character and circumstances of the people he trusts, and if he happens to be cheated, he knows better the laws of the country where he must seek redress. In the carrying trade, the merchant's capital is, in effect, split between two foreign countries, and no part of it ever has to come home or be placed under his own direct watch and control. The capital that an Amsterdam merchant uses to carry corn from Königsberg to Lisbon, and fruit and wine from Lisbon to Königsberg, must generally be half at Königsberg and half at Lisbon. None of it ever needs to reach Amsterdam. The natural place for such a merchant to live would be either Königsberg or Lisbon, and only very special circumstances could make him prefer Amsterdam. Still, the discomfort he feels at being so far from his capital usually drives him to route some of the Königsberg goods bound for Lisbon, and some of the Lisbon goods bound for Königsberg, through Amsterdam. This forces on him a double charge for loading and unloading, plus some duties and customs, yet for the sake of keeping part of his capital always under his own eye and command he willingly bears the extra cost. This is how any country with a sizeable share of the carrying trade always becomes the warehouse, or general marketplace, for the goods of all the different countries whose trade it carries. To save a second round of loading and unloading, the merchant always tries to sell as much of those various countries' goods as he can in the home market, converting his carrying trade, as far as possible, into a foreign trade in consumer goods. In the same way, a merchant engaged in the foreign trade in consumer goods, when he gathers goods for foreign markets, will always be glad—at equal or nearly equal profits—to sell as much of them at home as he can. By doing so he spares himself the risk and trouble of exporting, converting his foreign trade into a home trade as far as he can. Home, in this way, is the centre, so to speak, around which the capitals of a country's inhabitants are constantly circulating, and toward which they always tend, even though particular causes may sometimes drive them off toward more distant uses. But capital employed in the home trade, as already shown, necessarily sets in motion a greater quantity of domestic industry, and provides income and jobs to a greater number of the country's inhabitants, than an equal capital employed in the foreign trade in consumer goods; and capital in the foreign trade in consumer goods has the same advantage over an equal capital in the carrying trade. So at equal, or only nearly equal, profits every individual naturally tends to employ his capital in the way most likely to give the greatest support to domestic industry, and to provide income and jobs to the greatest number of his own countrymen.
Second, every individual who employs his capital in support of domestic industry necessarily tries to direct that industry so that its output is worth as much as possible.

The output of industry is whatever it adds to the object or materials it works on. The greater or smaller the value of that output, the greater or smaller the employer's profit will be. But the only reason any man employs capital in support of industry is profit, so he will always try to employ it in support of the industry whose output is likely to have the greatest value, or to exchange for the largest quantity of money or other goods.

Now, the annual revenue of any society is always exactly equal to the exchangeable value of the whole annual output of its industry—or rather, it is the very same thing as that exchangeable value. So since every individual tries as hard as he can both to employ his capital in support of domestic industry and to direct that industry so its output is worth the most, every individual necessarily works to make the society's annual revenue as great as he can. Generally, of course, he neither intends to promote the public interest nor knows how much he is promoting it. By preferring to support domestic rather than foreign industry, he is only looking to his own security; and by directing that industry so its output is worth the most, he is only looking to his own gain. In this, as in many other cases, he is led by an invisible hand to promote an end that was no part of his intention. And it is not always worse for society that this was no part of it. By pursuing his own interest he often promotes society's interest more effectively than when he actually means to. I have never known much good done by people who claimed to trade for the public good. It is an affectation, in fact, not very common among merchants, and very few words are needed to talk them out of it.

Which kind of domestic industry his capital can support, and which is likely to yield output of the greatest value, is something every individual can clearly judge far better in his own local situation than any statesman or lawmaker can judge for him. A statesman who tried to direct private people in how they should employ their capital would burden himself with quite unnecessary attention, and would claim an authority that could safely be trusted to no single person, no council, and no senate whatever—and that would nowhere be so dangerous as in the hands of a man foolish and presumptuous enough to imagine himself fit to wield it.

Giving the home-market monopoly to domestic industry in any particular craft or manufacture is, to some degree, to direct private people in how they should employ their capital, and in almost every case it must be either a useless or a harmful regulation. If domestic industry can supply the home market as cheaply as foreign industry can, the regulation is plainly useless. If it cannot, the regulation is generally harmful. It is the rule of every prudent head of a household never to try to make at home what would cost more to make than to buy. The tailor does not try to make his own shoes but buys them from the shoemaker. The shoemaker does not try to make his own clothes but employs a tailor. The farmer tries to make neither but employs both craftsmen. Each of them finds it in his interest to put all his effort into the line of work where he has some advantage over his neighbours, and to buy with part of his output—or, what comes to the same thing, with the price of part of it—whatever else he needs.

What is prudence in the conduct of any private family can hardly be folly in that of a great kingdom. If a foreign country can supply us with a good more cheaply than we can make it ourselves, we had better buy it from them with part of the output of our own industry, used in some line where we have an advantage. The country's total industry, always being in proportion to the capital that employs it, will not be reduced by this any more than the craftsmen's industry above; it will simply be left to find the use where it yields the greatest advantage. And it is certainly not being used to greatest advantage when it is directed toward something it could buy more cheaply than make. The value of the country's annual output is certainly reduced, more or less, when industry is turned away from producing goods that are plainly worth more than the good it is being directed to produce. By assumption, that good could be bought from abroad more cheaply than it could be made at home; it could therefore have been bought with only part of the goods—or, what comes to the same thing, with only part of the price of the goods—that the industry employed by an equal capital would have produced at home, had it been left to follow its natural course. So the country's industry is turned away from a more advantageous use to a less advantageous one, and the exchangeable value of its annual output, instead of rising as the lawmaker intended, must necessarily be reduced by every such regulation.

By means of such regulations, it is true, a particular manufacture may sometimes be acquired sooner than it otherwise would have been, and after a while may be made at home as cheaply as, or more cheaply than, in the foreign country. But even though the society's industry may thus be channeled with advantage into a particular line sooner than it otherwise would have been, it does not follow at all that the total of either its industry or its revenue can ever be increased by such a regulation. A society's industry can grow only in proportion as its capital grows, and its capital can grow only in proportion to what can gradually be saved out of its revenue. But the immediate effect of every such regulation is to reduce that revenue, and what reduces revenue is certainly not very likely to grow capital faster than it would have grown on its own, had both capital and industry been left to find their natural employments.

Even if, for lack of such regulations, the society never acquired the proposed manufacture, it would not on that account necessarily be poorer in any period of its existence. In every period its whole capital and industry could still have been employed, though on different things, in whatever way was most advantageous at the time. In every period its revenue could have been the greatest that its capital allowed, and both capital and revenue could have grown as fast as possible.

The natural advantages one country has over another in producing particular goods are sometimes so great that the whole world admits it is pointless to fight them. With glasshouses, hotbeds, and hot walls, very good grapes can be grown in Scotland, and very good wine made from them too—at about thirty times the cost of wine at least as good brought from abroad. Would it be a sensible law to ban the importation of all foreign wines merely to encourage the making of claret and burgundy in Scotland? But if it would be a plain absurdity to turn toward any line of work thirty times more of the country's capital and industry than would be needed to buy an equal quantity of the goods wanted from abroad, then it must also be an absurdity—not quite as glaring, but exactly of the same kind—to turn toward such a line a thirtieth, or even a three-hundredth, more. Whether the advantage one country has over another is natural or acquired makes no difference here. As long as one country has those advantages and the other lacks them, it will always be more advantageous for the second to buy from the first than to make. After all, it is only an acquired advantage that one craftsman has over his neighbour in a different trade, and yet they both find it more advantageous to buy from each other than to make what falls outside their own trades.

Merchants and manufacturers are the ones who gain the most from this home-market monopoly. The ban on importing foreign cattle and salted meat, together with the high duties on foreign corn that in years of moderate plenty amount to a ban, are nowhere near as advantageous to Britain's graziers and farmers as other regulations of the same kind are to its merchants and manufacturers. Manufactures, especially the finer sort, are more easily moved from one country to another than corn or cattle. So it is in fetching and carrying manufactures that foreign trade is mainly engaged. In manufactures, a very small advantage will let foreigners undersell our own workers even in the home market. It would take a very large one to let them do the same with the raw produce of the soil. If the free importation of foreign manufactures were allowed, several of our home manufactures would probably suffer, and some might be ruined altogether, and a good part of the capital and industry now employed in them would be forced to find some other use. But the freest importation of the raw produce of the soil could have no such effect on the country's agriculture.

If the importation of foreign cattle, for example, were made completely free, so few could be brought in that Britain's grazing trade would scarcely be affected. Live cattle are perhaps the only commodity whose transport is more expensive by sea than by land. By land they carry themselves to market. By sea, not only the cattle but their food and water too must be carried at no small cost and inconvenience. The short crossing between Ireland and Great Britain does make importing Irish cattle easier. But even if the free importation of them—recently allowed only for a limited time—were made permanent, it could have no significant effect on the interests of Britain's graziers. The parts of Britain bordering the Irish Sea are all grazing country. Irish cattle could never be imported for use there but would have to be driven through those very extensive grazing regions, at no small cost and inconvenience, before reaching their proper market. Fattened cattle could not be driven so far. Only lean cattle, then, could be imported, and such imports would interfere not with the feeding or fattening regions—to which, by lowering the price of lean cattle, they would actually be advantageous—but only with the breeding regions. The small number of Irish cattle imported since importation was allowed, together with the good price at which lean cattle still sell, seems to prove that even Britain's breeding regions are never likely to be much affected by the free importation of Irish cattle. The common people of Ireland, it is true, are said to have sometimes violently opposed the export of their cattle. But if the exporters had found any great advantage in keeping up the trade, they could easily, with the law on their side, have overcome that mob resistance.

Feeding and fattening regions, besides, must always be highly developed, whereas breeding regions are generally uncultivated. The high price of lean cattle, by raising the value of uncultivated land, acts like a reward against improvement. To a country that was highly developed throughout, it would be more advantageous to import its lean cattle than to breed them. The province of Holland is said to follow this rule at present. The mountains of Scotland, Wales, and Northumberland, it is true, are regions not capable of much improvement and seem destined by nature to be Britain's breeding grounds. The freest importation of foreign cattle could have no effect except to stop those breeding regions from cashing in on the growing population and improvement of the rest of the kingdom—from pushing their prices to an exorbitant height and laying a real tax on all the more improved and cultivated parts of the country.

The freest importation of salted meat, likewise, could affect the interests of Britain's graziers as little as that of live cattle. Salted meat is not only a very bulky commodity but, compared with fresh meat, it is of poorer quality, and, since it costs more labour and expense, of higher price. It could therefore never compete with fresh meat, though it might compete with the country's own salted meat. It might be used for provisioning ships on long voyages and similar uses, but could never make up any significant part of people's food. The small quantity of salted meat imported from Ireland since importation was made free is practical proof that our graziers have nothing to fear from it. There is no sign that the price of butcher's meat has ever been noticeably affected by it.

Even the free importation of foreign corn could affect the interests of Britain's farmers very little. Corn is a far bulkier commodity than butcher's meat. A pound of wheat at a penny is as dear as a pound of butcher's meat at fourpence. The small quantity of foreign corn imported even in times of greatest scarcity may convince our farmers that they have nothing to fear from the freest importation. The average quantity imported, one year with another, comes—according to the very well-informed author of the Tracts upon the Corn Trade—to only 23,728 quarters of all kinds of grain, which is no more than one five-hundred-and-seventy-first of annual consumption. But since the bounty on corn causes greater exports in years of plenty, it must correspondingly cause greater imports in years of scarcity than would otherwise occur given the actual state of farming. Because of it, the plenty of one year does not make up for the scarcity of another; and as the average quantity exported is necessarily raised by it, so too, given the actual state of farming, must be the average quantity imported. Without the bounty, less corn would be exported, and it is likely that, one year with another, less would also be imported than at present. The corn merchants—the fetchers and carriers of corn between Britain and foreign countries—would have much less to do and might suffer considerably; but country gentlemen and farmers could suffer very little. It is among the corn merchants, accordingly, rather than the country gentlemen and farmers, that I have noticed the greatest eagerness for renewing and continuing the bounty.

Country gentlemen and farmers are, to their great credit, the least prone of all people to the wretched spirit of monopoly. The owner of a great manufactory is sometimes alarmed if another works of the same kind is set up within twenty miles of him; the Dutch owner of the woollen works at Abbeville stipulated that no works of the same kind should be set up within thirty leagues of that city. Farmers and country gentlemen, by contrast, are generally inclined to promote rather than block the cultivation and improvement of their neighbours' farms and estates. They have no trade secrets, as most manufacturers do, but are generally rather fond of sharing with their neighbours, and of spreading as widely as possible any new practice they have found useful. "Pius quaestus," says old Cato, "stabilissimusque, minimeque invidiosus; minimeque male cogitantes sunt, qui in eo studio occupati sunt." Country gentlemen and farmers, scattered across different parts of the country, cannot combine as easily as merchants and manufacturers, who, being gathered into towns and used to the exclusive corporate spirit that prevails there, naturally try to win against all their countrymen the same exclusive privilege they generally hold against the inhabitants of their own towns. They accordingly seem to have been the original inventors of those restraints on importing foreign goods that secure them the home-market monopoly. It was probably in imitation of them, and to put themselves on a par with people they saw were ready to oppress them, that Britain's country gentlemen and farmers so far forgot the generosity natural to their station as to demand the exclusive privilege of supplying their countrymen with corn and butcher's meat. Perhaps they did not take time to consider how much less their own interest would be affected by free trade than that of the people whose example they followed.

To ban, by a permanent law, the importation of foreign corn and cattle is really to decree that the country's population and industry shall never exceed what the raw produce of its own soil can support.
There seem, however, to be two cases in which it will generally be advantageous to lay some burden on foreign industry in order to encourage domestic industry.

The first is when some particular kind of industry is necessary for the country's defence. Britain's defence, for example, depends very much on the number of its sailors and ships. The Act of Navigation therefore quite properly tries to give British sailors and ships a monopoly over their own country's trade—in some cases by outright bans, in others by heavy burdens on foreign shipping. Here are the act's main provisions.

First, all ships whose owners, masters, and three-quarters of the crew are not British subjects are forbidden, on pain of forfeiting ship and cargo, from trading to British settlements and plantations, or from being used in Britain's coastal trade.

Second, a great many of the bulkiest imported articles can be brought into Britain only in ships of the kind just described, or in ships of the country where those goods are produced—ships whose owners, masters, and three-quarters of the crew belong to that particular country—and even when imported in ships of this latter kind they are subject to double aliens' duty. If imported in ships of any other country, the penalty is forfeiture of ship and goods. When this act was passed, the Dutch were, as they still are, the great carriers of Europe, and this regulation entirely shut them out from being Britain's carriers or from importing to us the goods of any other European country.

Third, a great many of the bulkiest imported articles are forbidden to be imported, even in British ships, from any country except the one where they are produced, on pain of forfeiting ship and cargo. This regulation, too, was probably aimed at the Dutch. Holland was then, as now, the great warehouse for all European goods, and this regulation stopped British ships from loading in Holland the goods of any other European country.

Fourth, salt fish of all kinds, whale fins, whalebone, oil, and blubber not caught and cured aboard British vessels are subject to double aliens' duty when imported into Britain. The Dutch, who are still the chief fishers in Europe, were then the only ones who tried to supply foreign nations with fish. This regulation laid a very heavy burden on their supplying Britain.

When the Act of Navigation was passed, though England and Holland were not actually at war, the most violent animosity existed between the two nations. It had begun under the Long Parliament, which first drew up this act, and it broke out soon after in the Dutch wars, under the Protector and Charles II. It is therefore not impossible that some of this famous act's provisions sprang from national animosity. They are as wise, however, as if they had all been dictated by the most deliberate wisdom. At that particular moment, national animosity aimed at the very same goal that the most deliberate wisdom would have recommended: weakening the naval power of Holland, the only naval power that could threaten England's security.

The Act of Navigation is not favourable to foreign commerce, or to the growth of wealth that can arise from it. A nation's interest in its commercial dealings with foreign nations is, like a merchant's interest with the various people he deals with, to buy as cheaply and sell as dearly as possible. But it is most likely to buy cheaply when, through the most perfect freedom of trade, it encourages all nations to bring it the goods it needs to buy; and, for the same reason, it is most likely to sell dearly when its markets are thus filled with the greatest number of buyers. The Act of Navigation, it is true, lays no burden on foreign ships that come to export the produce of British industry. Even the old aliens' duty, once paid on all goods both exported and imported, has been removed by several later acts from most export articles. But if foreigners are kept from coming to sell, whether by bans or high duties, they often cannot afford to come to buy either, because, coming without a cargo, they would lose the freight from their own country to Britain. By reducing the number of sellers, then, we necessarily reduce the number of buyers, and so are likely not only to buy foreign goods more dearly but also to sell our own more cheaply than if trade were freer. But since defence matters far more than wealth, the Act of Navigation is perhaps the wisest of all England's commercial regulations.

The second case in which it will generally be advantageous to lay some burden on foreign industry to encourage domestic industry is when a tax is imposed at home on domestic output. Here it seems reasonable to impose an equal tax on the same kind of foreign output. This would not give the home market to domestic industry, nor turn toward a particular line of work a larger share of the country's capital and labour than would naturally go there. It would only stop part of what would naturally go there from being diverted by the tax into a less natural direction, and would leave the competition between foreign and domestic industry, after the tax, as nearly as possible on the same footing as before it. In Britain, when such a tax is laid on domestic output, it is usual at the same time—to silence the loud complaints of our merchants and manufacturers that they will be undersold at home—to lay a much heavier duty on the importation of all foreign goods of the same kind.

This second limitation on free trade, according to some people, should usually be extended far beyond the precise foreign goods that could compete with those taxed at home. When the necessities of life have been taxed in a country, they claim, it becomes proper to tax not only the same necessities imported from abroad but all sorts of foreign goods that could compete with anything produced by domestic industry. Subsistence, they say, necessarily becomes dearer as a result of such taxes, and the price of labour must always rise with the price of the labourer's subsistence. So every commodity produced by domestic industry, even if it is not directly taxed itself, becomes dearer because of such taxes, since the labour that produces it becomes dearer. Such taxes, they say, are therefore really equivalent to a tax on every single commodity produced at home. To put domestic industry on the same footing as foreign industry, then, they think it necessary to lay on every foreign commodity a duty equal to this rise in the price of the home commodities it can compete with.

Whether taxes on the necessities of life—such as those in Britain on soap, salt, leather, candles, and so on—necessarily raise the price of labour, and consequently of all other commodities, I shall consider later when I come to deal with taxes. But suppose for now that they do have this effect, as they undoubtedly do; this general rise in the price of all commodities, caused by the dearer labour, differs in the two following respects from the case of a particular commodity whose price is raised by a particular tax imposed directly on it.

First, it can always be known very exactly how far the price of such a commodity could be raised by such a tax; but how far the general rise in the price of labour might affect the price of every different commodity that labour helps produce could never be known with any tolerable accuracy. It would therefore be impossible to match, with any tolerable accuracy, the tax on every foreign commodity to the rise in price of every home commodity.

Second, taxes on the necessities of life have nearly the same effect on people's circumstances as poor soil and a bad climate. They make provisions dearer, just as if it took extra labour and expense to grow them.
